title: School Leadership and Governance in Kenya: A 2026 Guide
h1: School Leadership and Governance in Kenya: A 2026 Guide
description: School leadership and governance in Kenya — roles of the board, head, deputies and bursar, decision-making, reporting, accountability and managing change.
author: SQUL Team
intro: Most school problems are, at root, governance problems: unclear roles, decisions nobody owns, and reporting that arrives too late. Fix the governance and the operational fires put themselves out. This guide covers **school leadership and governance in Kenya** — who decides what, how to report, and how to keep accountability alive. It is part of our wider guide on [how to manage a school in Kenya](/blog/how-to-manage-a-school-in-kenya).
It applies to public schools with a Board of Management and to private schools with a board of directors.

blocks.text: Governance fails in two directions: a board that micromanages daily operations, or a head who reports nothing and owns everything. Clear roles prevent both.

rows: Direction, policy, budget approval, holding the head accountable
Run the timetable or hire day-to-day staff
Daily running, staff, learners, curriculum delivery, spending within budget

items: **Name the decision owner** — every recurring decision needs exactly one.
**Match authority to responsibility** — if the head is accountable, give them enough authority.
**Decide at the right level** — classroom vs department vs whole school.
**Write decisions down** — a short minute prevents later disagreement.

blocks.text: Accountability is a rhythm, not an annual event. A predictable cycle of meetings and reports builds board confidence and catches problems early.

rows: Budget, fee structure, results, strategic plan

blocks.text: The termly board pack should be short and consistent: enrolment, results, finances (income vs expectation, spend vs budget), arrears, staffing, and risks. See [school finance and budgeting](/blog/school-finance-and-budgeting-kenya).

items: **Be consistent** — the same rule for the same situation, every time.
**Be transparent about money** — parents and staff accept what they can see.
**Protect staff dignity** — correct privately, praise publicly.
**Follow through** — an unkept promise costs more than the original issue.

items.title: Explain the why
items.text: People resist change they do not understand — especially staff and parents.

items.title: Start where it hurts most
items.text: Fees and communication usually deliver the earliest, most visible wins.

items.title: Show the result quickly
items.text: A same-day fee receipt changes minds faster than a policy document.

items.title: Make it routine
items.text: Change sticks when it becomes the default, not an initiative.

blocks.text: A head teacher cannot run everything alone. Delegate to a deputy, HODs and the bursar, and give each a clear mandate and the tools to do it. See [managing teachers and staff](/blog/school-staff-management-kenya) for the people side.

items: **Board in the weeds** — directors arguing about timetables.
**Head owns everything** — no delegation, nothing reported.
**No meeting rhythm** — decisions made in corridors.
**Reporting too late** — the board learns of problems after they bite.

faqs.question: What is the role of a Board of Management in a Kenyan school?
faqs.answer: The board sets direction, approves policy and the budget, and holds the head teacher accountable. It does not run daily operations such as timetabling or routine staffing.

faqs.question: What is the head teacher responsible for?
faqs.answer: The head runs the school day to day: staff, learners, curriculum delivery, and spending within the approved budget, while reporting to the board.

faqs.question: How often should a school board meet?
faqs.answer: A common rhythm is monthly on finance and procurement, plus a termly board meeting on results, finances, staffing and risks, with an annual review of budget and strategy.

faqs.question: How do we improve accountability in a school?
faqs.answer: Name a decision owner for every recurring decision, match authority to responsibility, keep a meeting and reporting rhythm, and be consistent and transparent — especially about money.

faqs.question: How should leadership handle change?
faqs.answer: Explain the why, start where it hurts most (usually fees and communication), show an early visible win, then make the new way the default.
